Article Title: Amit Shah outlines ambitions for Gujarat as sports powerhouse; 19 nations participate in World Archery Para Series
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Home minister Amit Shah on Friday said India will soon become a major centre for all activities linked to sports, be it hosting international games including Olympics, emerging as a sports training and coaching hub that will cater to both national and international sportspersons, or for management of sports injuries.Addressing the inauguration ceremony of the World Archery Para Series, being organised in Ahmedabad from Sept 5 to 9, via video-conferencing, Shah extended a warm welcome to around 108 para-athletes from 19 nations who will participate in the championship."This event will generate great memories for both you and Ahmedabad....In the days to come, Ahmedabad, Gujarat and Bharat are set to emerge as key centres for hosting major international games like Olympics and paralympics and for various sporting activities, sports training, sports facilities and also manufacturing of sports equipment. As part of this complete vision, under the leadership of Narendra Modi ji, India is moving forward to become the biggest global hub for sports," he stated.Shah said the intention behind organising the world archery para-series was not just to win medals but to promote sports being played as part of Olympics, Asian, Commonwealth and police games. "The major sports coaching facilities being developed in Ahmedabad will not just benefit local and domestic players; they are being developed as per international standards and will cater to sportspersons from across the world.In the days to come, India will become a global pioneer in the sports injury field of medical science, and Gujarat will become its major hub" said the home minister.While welcoming the international para-athletes and extending best wishes to Indian participants, Shah said he was confident that Ahmedabad, which has hosted 10 international sporting events over the past decade and shall also be hosting the 100th edition of the Commonwealth Games, will also win the bid to host the 2036 Olympic Games."The archery paraseries is a good opportunity for you to know India and Gujarat," he said while advising the international sportspersons to visit and experience tourist attractions like Somnath temple, Ekta Nagar and Dwarka.Nineteen nations including Bhutan, China, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Indonesia and the US are participating in the archery championship.

Article Title: Chiefs' billionaire heiress Gracie Hunt refuses to follow the family script as she builds her own empire
Article Text:
Gracie Hunt is carving out her own identity beyond the Chiefs

Gracie Hunt’s fashion and philanthropy ventures stand on their own

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Being born into NFL royalty can open almost every door, but it can also make it difficult to prove that you belong in the room for your own reasons. Gracie Hunt knows that tension well. As the daughter of Kansas City Chiefs chairman and CEO Clark Hunt and granddaughter of franchise founder Lamar Hunt, football has always surrounded her. Yet her ambitions have grown far beyond the family business.Hunt could easily have made the Chiefs her entire professional world. Instead, she has built a portfolio that reflects interests she developed long before stepping into the family spotlight.Her journey began with soccer. As a child, she dreamed of following in the footsteps of Mia Hamm and even played the sport through high school. Her family connection to soccer ran deep, too, with her grandfather playing a role in bringing Major League Soccer to the United States.That dream changed after she suffered several concussions. Rather than allowing the setback to define her, Hunt found another competitive outlet in pageantry. She eventually won Miss Kansas USA in 2021, following an example set by her mother, Tavia Hunt, who won the same title in 1993.Her career since then has blended sports, fashion, philanthropy and advocacy. She has worked with the Chiefs Women’s Organization, supported community initiatives and explored opportunities that exist outside the football franchise."The things that have been really important to me my whole life have been faith, family, football and philanthropy," Gracie says. "Because I've always been raised with the mantra that, 'To whom much is given, much is expected'."That philosophy has helped shape the way she views her position. For Hunt, having access to the Chiefs is not necessarily a reason to claim ownership of its spotlight."When it comes to the Chiefs, there's no 'I' in 'team'. It's not about me," Gracie makes clear.One of Hunt’s clearest efforts to establish an independent identity came through fashion. Her collaboration with broadcaster Erin Andrews gave her an opportunity to create something that was not simply connected to the Chiefs or her family."Coming out with a capsule collection with Erin was a way for me to create something that is my own," Gracie says.She explained why that distinction mattered."Obviously it's in partnership with Wear, so it's our own — but it wasn't a Chiefs project or a family initiative," she says. "It was a Gracie Hunt initiative and something that I cared about, that I spent a lot of time creating and hoping that women would love as much as I did."Her work with the Chiefs community remains important, especially the charitable efforts she experienced alongside her mother. From supporting people facing homelessness and hunger to helping build homes with Habitat for Humanity, Hunt has treated philanthropy as more than a public title.She also champions the growing influence of women in NFL fashion, pointing to designers and Chiefs WAGs who are expanding the options available to female fans.That balance may be the most interesting part of Hunt’s story. She has no need to reject her family legacy to establish herself. Instead, she is using the opportunities around her while building a career that carries her own name."I am certainly so fulfilled by all the things that I have created for myself opportunity-wise outside of football. But it's been a pleasure to be of some part of something that's greater than myself, to serve where there's room and need and to be their number one fan," she says of the Kansas City Chiefs.
Article Summary: Gracie hunt is the daughter of kansas city chiefs chairman and ceo clark hunt and granddaughter of franchise founder lamar hunt. Hunt could easily have made the chiefs her entire professional world. Instead, she has built a portfolio that reflects interests she developed long before stepping into the family spotlight.

Article Title: Career turning point: “I’m not a Serena fan. I’m just a tennis player”: How Naomi Osaka’s emotional US Open win over Serena Williams changed her career forever, making her a global star
Article Text:
How Naomi Osaka’s emotional US Open win over Serena Williams changed her career forever, making her a global star(Getty Images)

How did beating Serena Williams become Naomi Osaka’s career turning point?

How did the 2018 US Open change Naomi Osaka’s career?

Why does Serena Williams remain central to Naomi Osaka’s career story?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Naomi Osaka arrived at the 2018 US Open as a talented 20-year-old who had already shown she could trouble the biggest names in tennis. What happened in New York, however, turned her from a rising star into a Grand Slam champion.Her 6-2, 6-4 victory over Serena Williams in the final was more than Osaka’s first major title. It became the defining moment of her career and the match that introduced her to a global audience in a way no previous result had done.The signs that Osaka was ready for a major breakthrough had already appeared earlier in 2018. She won her first WTA title at Indian Wells, beating Daria Kasatkina 6-3, 6-2 in the final after defeating Maria Sharapova, Agnieszka Radwanska, Karolina Pliskova and world No. 1 Simona Halep during the tournament. The run pushed her into the world’s top 25 and gave her the confidence to believe she could compete with the best players on the biggest stages.The US Open, though, presented a completely different challenge. Osaka entered the tournament as the No. 20 seed and reached her first Grand Slam final without dropping a set in the semifinal against Madison Keys. She beat the American 6-2, 6-4 and saved all 13 break points she faced, becoming the first Japanese woman in the Open Era to reach a Grand Slam singles final.Waiting for her was Serena, the player Osaka had admired since childhood. Osaka had never hidden what Serena meant to her. Before the final, she explained that she had dreamed about facing Williams on a Grand Slam stage since she was a child. Yet she also understood that treating the final like a fan could make the occasion overwhelming, so she tried to separate her admiration from the task in front of her.“Even when I was a little kid, I always dreamed that I would play Serena in a final of a Grand Slam,” Osaka said before the match.She then added, “At the same time I feel like even though I should enjoy this moment, I should still think of it as another match. I shouldn't really think of her as my idol. I should just try to play her as an opponent.”That approach showed immediately. Osaka played with remarkable control, breaking Serena early in the first set and refusing to allow the occasion to dictate her tennis. She won the opening set 6-2 and carried that momentum into the second.The final became increasingly tense because of the controversy surrounding Serena and chair umpire Carlos Ramos. Williams received a code violation for coaching, followed by a point penalty after breaking her racquet and a game penalty after being assessed a verbal abuse violation. The situation created a hostile atmosphere inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, but Osaka continued trying to stay focused on the match.She eventually closed it out 6-2, 6-4 on her second championship point.The credentials showed just how composed she had been. Osaka hit six aces, saved five of six break points and converted four of five break opportunities against Williams. More importantly, she never allowed the drama around the court to pull her completely away from the job.That was what made the victory such a major turning point. Osaka did not simply beat one of the greatest players in tennis. She handled the pressure of playing her childhood idol, the weight of a Grand Slam final and an increasingly emotional atmosphere, all before turning 21.After the match, Osaka famously said, “When I step onto the court, I feel like a different person. I’m not a Serena fan. I’m just a tennis player playing another tennis player. But then when I hugged her at the net, I felt like a little kid again.”That quote captured the strange reality of the night. On the court, Osaka had played Serena as an opponent. At the net, she was still the young girl who had grown up watching her.The title immediately changed Osaka’s position in tennis. Before New York, she was a promising young player with one WTA title. After New York, she was a Grand Slam champion and one of the biggest names in the sport.She also became the first Japanese player, male or female, to win a Grand Slam singles title. That achievement gave her a place in Japanese tennis history while also establishing her as one of the leading players of her generation.The victory over Serena was not an isolated success either. Osaka followed it by winning the 2019 Australian Open, where she defeated Petra Kvitova in the final. That second major title made her the first Japanese player to reach the No. 1 ranking in the WTA rankings.Her rise continued at the 2020 US Open. Osaka defeated Victoria Azarenka in the final after recovering from a set and a break down to claim her third Grand Slam title. In 2021, she won the Australian Open again, beating Jennifer Brady in the final for her fourth major championship.That sequence changed the way Osaka was viewed. The 2018 US Open was no longer simply a surprising breakthrough. It became the beginning of a period in which she established herself as a genuine Grand Slam force.Her success also gave her a much larger platform away from tennis. Osaka became one of the most recognizable athletes in the world, with her public profile growing alongside her results. Her willingness to speak openly about pressure, expectations and life away from the court also made her a prominent figure far beyond tennis.Yet the significance of the 2018 final goes deeper than the trophies that followed. It showed Osaka that she could handle a moment that looked almost impossibly large. She was facing a player she had idolized, in front of a packed New York crowd, with her first Grand Slam title within reach. Instead of allowing the occasion to overwhelm her, she trusted the tennis that had taken her there.Osaka herself later reflected on how quickly her life changed after winning Indian Wells and then the US Open. In 2026, she recalled that after Indian Wells she thought life could not get much crazier because the victory had helped her mother retire. Then the US Open brought another level of change.That progression helps explain why New York remains such an important part of her career story. Indian Wells proved Osaka could beat elite players. The US Open proved she could do it when everything around the match became enormous.Serena’s importance to Osaka’s story did not disappear after that final. If anything, the match created a connection between the two players that became part of Osaka’s identity.The most striking part was how Osaka viewed Serena even after becoming the person who had defeated her in a Grand Slam final. The result did not erase the admiration she had carried since childhood.“The thing is, I don't know what happened on the court. So for me, I'm always going to remember the Serena that I love,” Osaka said after the final. “It doesn't change anything for me.”That sentiment explained why the victory was so emotional for her. Osaka had achieved the dream she had once imagined as a young fan, but the person standing across the net was still someone she respected deeply.At the same time, Osaka understood that beating Serena meant she had to create her own identity. She later put that balance into simple words: “She’ll always be someone I look up to. But tennis-wise, I want to try to do my own thing. I want to be my own person.”That became an important theme of Osaka’s career. She was no longer simply the player who admired Serena Williams. She had become a champion with her own place in tennis.Still, when looking for the single moment that changed the direction of her career, the answer remains clear. Indian Wells announced Osaka to the tennis world, but the 2018 US Open final changed her status forever.She entered Arthur Ashe Stadium as a 20-year-old playing her childhood idol. She left it as a Grand Slam champion and the first Japanese player to win a major singles title. The controversy surrounding the final became part of its history, but Osaka’s tennis was what ultimately defined the night.Hence, the 2018 US Open remains the clearest career turning point for Naomi Osaka. It was the night she stopped being the promising young player everyone was watching and became the champion everyone had to watch.
Article Summary: Naomi osaka beat serena williams 6-2, 6-4 in the 2018 us open final. It was the first grand slam title for the 20-year-old japanese tennis player. The match introduced osaka to a global audience in a way no previous result had. Osaka became the first japanese player, male or female, to win a grand slam singles title.

T20I career so far

Abhishek Sharma has come a long way from the little boy in Amritsar who first picked up a cricket bat at the age of three-and-a-half. On his birthday, his journey stands out as one of the most remarkable rises in modern T20 cricket, from a promising youngster in Punjab to an India regular and the holder of the highest-ever ICC T20I batting rating.Abhishek's father, Raj Kumar Sharma, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game when he was just three-and-a-half. The youngster quickly developed an obsession with batting and progressed through Punjab's age-group system.His numbers soon began attracting attention. During the 2015-16 Vijay Merchant Trophy, Abhishek scored more than 1,200 runs at an average of 109.09 and also claimed 57 wickets. He captained Punjab to the Under-19 Asia Cup title in 2016 before becoming part of India's victorious Under-19 World Cup campaign in 2018.The IPL came at just 17, when Delhi Daredevils picked him in the 2018 auction. His career, however, did not explode immediately. Abhishek spent several seasons developing his game through domestic cricket and the IPL before finding the perfect platform for his aggressive style.A major influence during that period was Yuvraj Singh. The former India all-rounder became Abhishek's mentor and worked closely with him, particularly during the Covid-19 lockdown.Yuvraj understood the youngster's attacking instincts and encouraged him to embrace them rather than become overly cautious. That philosophy eventually became the foundation of Abhishek's T20 game.His international breakthrough came after making his T20I debut in July 2024. In February 2025, Abhishek produced one of the most devastating T20I innings by an Indian batter when he smashed 135 off just 54 balls against England in Mumbai. The innings contained 13 sixes and a 37-ball century, announcing him as one of India's most dangerous T20 batters.The 135 was only the beginning. During the 2025 Asia Cup, Abhishek established himself as India's attacking force at the top of the order. He scored 314 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of 200 and was named Player of the Tournament as India won the competition.His performances pushed him to the top of the ICC T20I batting rankings and eventually into record-breaking territory. After scoring 61 against Sri Lanka, Abhishek reached 931 rating points, the highest-ever rating achieved by a men's T20I batter.He surpassed Dawid Malan's previous record of 919 and moved beyond the best ratings achieved by India's Suryakumar Yadav and Virat Kohli.The numbers behind Abhishek's rise were extraordinary. In 2025, he became the first player to score more than 1,000 runs in T20 cricket in a calendar year while maintaining a strike rate above 200. He finished the year at a strike rate of 202 and smashed 108 sixes.His IPL performances were equally destructive. Playing for Sunrisers Hyderabad, Abhishek produced a stunning 141 off 55 balls against Punjab Kings in IPL 2025. He reached his fifty in only 16 balls and his century in 40, hitting 14 fours and 10 sixes as Hyderabad chased down 246. The innings broke KL Rahul's record for the highest score by an Indian batter in IPL history.His development has been shaped by several influential figures. Apart from Yuvraj, Abhishek has drawn lessons from players such as Shikhar Dhawan, Brian Lara and Travis Head. At Sunrisers, his partnership with Head showed how effectively his aggressive approach could work against the best bowling attacks.At the 2026 T20 World Cup, Abhishek added another major achievement to his growing list, playing a crucial role in India's title-winning campaign, including a blistering 52 off 21 balls in the final against New Zealand.Abhishek Sharma has played 56 T20Is between 2024 and 2026, scoring 1,629 runs in 55 innings at an average of 30.73 and a remarkable strike rate of 187.24. He has registered two centuries and 11 fifties, with a highest score of 135. His aggressive approach is reflected in his boundary count, with the left-hander hitting 164 fours and 104 sixes in his international career so far.
Article Summary: Abhishek sharma started playing cricket at the age of three-and-a-half. His father, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game. NEW DELHI: Anshuman Hooda bursts into laughter when asked to choose between his office laptop and his cricket ball. “My cricket ball is my best friend,” he tells TimesofIndia.com.His elder brother, Vikram Hooda, says their mother, Prem Lata Singh, a primary class teacher at a Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) school, is happy to see Anshuman pursue cricket, especially now that he has a stable job. “Earlier, they used to say that he needed a job. Now that he has one and is doing well, she is happy,” Vikram says of their parents.Anshuman had a breakout 2026 Delhi Premier League (DPL) season -- emerging as the Purple Cap winner with 22 scalps -- which played a crucial role in South Delhi Superstarz's title triumph.But there was a time when Hooda thought cricket had run its course. Two attempts at the Under-23 trials had gone by without success. There was no age-group cricket on his résumé, no traditional pathway through Delhi's junior system and no obvious route into first-class cricket. He had an engineering degree from Delhi Technological University (DTU) and a job at EY. The sensible thing, he thought, was to move on.“I tried for Under-23 for two years, but I couldn’t make it. I thought it would be very difficult because I hadn’t played any professional cricket or age-group cricket.It would have been very difficult to directly get selected for the Ranji Trophy or first-class cricket,” Anshuman recollects.“So at that time, I thought I should quit cricket and pursue my career in engineering or something.”But just when he thought of walking away from the game, his coach Harish Dagar, who runs a cricket academy named Delhi Cricket Hub in Delhi's Paschim Vihar, and trains youngsters at DTU, stepped up.“It was in 2023. He had just graduated. He had got the job through campus placement and was ready to move on with his life. I pleaded with him to give it one more year. I asked him to come to my academy four days a week for a year, and if nothing would pan out, I would let him pursue his corporate job,” reminisces Dagar.Then came the Delhi Premier League (DPL). And with it came a completely different possibility. For a young man who had arrived late to leather-ball cricket, DPL became the stage on which his raw pace, athleticism and appetite for fast bowling could finally be seen. The numbers followed. The attention followed, and now Anshuman is finally ready to become a full-time cricketer.“I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament. So in the coming times, I might shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all,” he says.Anshuman is 25 and, in cricketing terminology, he can be called a late bloomer. But the most unusual thing about Anshuman's story is perhaps where it began. Not with a cricket academy. Not with a junior tournament. Not with a childhood obsession with bowling. With roller skates.Growing up, Anshuman was a national-level roller skater. Cricket existed around him, but it was not initially the sport that defined him. His elder brother Vikram had played cricket, and there was, as Anshuman puts it, a familiar sibling dynamic. His brother took science. He took science. His brother studied engineering. He studied engineering. But when it came to cricket, Anshuman's journey took its own route.It was only when he reached college that the game began to take hold.“I just started playing in college, and that’s when I got into leather-ball cricket professionally, playing for the college team and all. That’s when I fell in love with bowling fast, getting wickets and the aggression that comes with it. I just loved bowling fast.”That love became the starting point of something neither his résumé nor his previous sporting journey could have predicted.Harish Dagar first noticed Anshuman in 2019 while they were at university. What caught his eye was not a polished fast bowler. It was the physical package.Fitness. Arm speed. Natural movement.Anshuman was playing tennis-ball cricket when Dagar asked him to try medium pace. The first attempts were raw and erratic, but there was enough pace and athletic ability for the coach to believe there was something worth developing.“His body alignment was natural. His strength was natural, and his pace was natural. But he didn't have enough strength in his body initially. That's why I told him that if you don't maintain your fitness along with your natural pace, you will face problems," says Dagar.“He was also busy with his job. He couldn't always take proper sessions. He would come at night, then have to go to the gym and take practice sessions. It was very hectic.“I worked on his mind 80-85 per cent. I made him mentally strong. I told him never to think that he was tired or burdened.“Once I worked on his mindset and the roadmap was clear in front of him, he knew what he had to do. At one point he had to focus on fitness, at another he had to do his job, and then he had to come to me for his sessions."Anshuman graduated from DTU with a degree in Production and Industrial Engineering and joined a multinational company in 2023. He worked from home, which helped him juggle the demands of employment and an increasingly serious cricket career. But balancing the two was never going to be easy.Fast bowling is an unforgiving craft. It demands strength, recovery, repetition and hours of training. Dagar's approach was to build Anshuman patiently, focusing not merely on speed but on the physical and mental foundations that could allow him to bowl fast consistently.Anshuman also had to understand his own body. He had dealt with niggles and the physical toll that comes with repeatedly accelerating, landing and transferring his entire body weight through a bowling action.“Fast bowling is not a very comfortable activity for the body. You accelerate, then your whole body has to absorb the impact before you bowl. It definitely takes a toll on the body,” he says.But there was no great mystery behind his motivation. He adds: “It was just the love for the sport and the love for bowling fast that kept me motivated and helped me come back stronger every time.”That attitude has been central to his development.Dagar describes the next stage of the process in more professional terms: periodisation, rest, strength work, workload scheduling, diet, physiotherapy and technical skills. Anshuman had to develop a stock ball and variations such as the leg-cutter and off-cutter while ensuring that his body could cope with the demands of pace.The objective was never simply to produce a fast delivery. It was to produce a fast bowler. The first real crack in the wall came through the DPL.In 2024, he got his opportunity with South Delhi, initially finding chances hard to come by. Then came a spell that changed perceptions. The next season brought more opportunities, including a five-wicket haul, and soon IPL franchises were looking at him as a net bowler and trial candidate.The journey from someone contemplating quitting cricket to someone attracting franchise attention had happened remarkably quickly. For Anshuman, the attention became tangible when Shikhar Dhawan , the owner of his DPL team, spoke to him after his performances.“Shikhar Dhawan himself, the team owner, surprised me. He came and we had a little conversation. He gave me some very good tips and a direction to work towards from here,” he says.It was a moment of validation. For someone who had spent years outside the conventional cricket pathway, being noticed by an established name carried significance beyond a conversation.At 140 kmph, Anshuman possesses the one commodity that can change a fast bowler's career quickly: pace. Coach Dagar believes there is more to come. Anshuman is not shy about wanting it.“Definitely, speed is what I want. If I can, I will definitely look to bowl even faster and build the strength and skills to do that, while making sure there is no compromise on accuracy and line,” said Anshuman.That final clause is important. Pace can attract attention. Accuracy keeps a fast bowler in a team. For Anshuman, the next challenge is therefore not simply touching a bigger number on the speed gun. It is learning how to sustain high pace across long spells, particularly in red-ball cricket.He is already thinking about it. “These are the things we prepare for. Who bowls in a four-day or five-day game and bowls long spells with the same effort? That is what I am preparing for. If I get an opportunity, I will definitely do that.”Anshuman's ambition is clear. First, Delhi. Then first-class cricket. Then, eventually, IPL and India.“The eventual goal is to play and win matches for the country. That is my ultimate goal,” he says.There is, however, one more conversation happening in Anshuman's life. The conversation between security and possibility. An engineering degree and a job at a good company offer a predictable future. And he has got a promotion before the start of the DPL season as well. Cricket offers something very different: uncertainty, competition and the possibility of a career that can disappear as quickly as it arrives.For now, Anshuman has returned to work. But his cricket has progressed to the point where continuing to divide himself between the two may no longer be possible.“Currently, I have joined back. But as I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament, I might, in the coming times, shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all.”It is a significant sentence from someone who once thought about quitting the sport altogether. There is also a quiet irony in the fact that the engineer who learned to manage competing demands may soon have to choose one.Anshuman knows where he wants to go.“I will give it my all. Let’s see what happens ahead.”
Article Summary: Anshuman hooda picked up 22 wickets in the third edition of the delhi premier league. The 25-year-old is also an engineer by profession. “my cricket ball is my best friend,” he tells timesofindia. Anshuman was a national-level roller skater. His elder brother vikram had played cricket, and there was a familiar sibling dynamic.

Article Title: 'Serving country against biological clock': Spain to fund egg freezing for women football players; what does it mean?
Article Text:
Mariona Caldentey, Irene Paredes, Alexia Putellas, Claudia Pina and Olga Carmona look on during a training session at RCDE Stadium on June 02, 2025 in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo/Getty Images)

Players raised the issue with the federation

What egg freezing means for elite athletes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

No clear rules yet in women's football

Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers, in a move aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level.According to a report by EL Pais, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) is finalising an agreement with a fertility clinic that will allow members of the Spain women's team to undergo egg vitrification. The agreement is expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.The move comes as more women athletes face the challenge of fitting pregnancy into long sporting careers. A football career can continue into a player's thirties, but pregnancy often means several months away from training and competition, and returning to the highest level can be difficult.Former Spain captain Alexia Putellas said the team's captains had discussed the issue with the federation and welcomed the proposal."The federation understands that you are serving your country against your biological clock, that you cannot stop and cannot be a mother because you need your body to work," Putellas was quoted as saying by EL Pais."The group of captains had a concern because it is very important for a player to experience World Cups, but that means that those of us who have the desire to become mothers do not find it easy to fit it in."The federation has not yet confirmed whether it will cover the full treatment, only the egg preservation process, or also the egg retrieval procedure.Sports medicine specialist Eva Ferrer said egg vitrification has become a topic of discussion in women's football only over the past couple of years.She explained that there is still limited research on how ovarian stimulation affects athletes. "There are not enough studies on how the treatment [ovarian stimulation] could affect, for example, the joints or soft tissue," Ferrer said as quoted by EL Pais.She added that training may need to be adjusted during treatment to reduce the risk of injury. She also said the medications used during the process must be declared through a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) so athletes do not face anti-doping issues.The treatment usually lasts about two weeks. During that period, the player injects hormonal medication to stimulate the ovaries so multiple eggs mature instead of one. Doctors then retrieve the eggs through a procedure performed under sedation.After the procedure, players may experience bleeding, discomfort, swelling, fluid retention, migraines and lower energy levels while the ovaries recover. Clinics generally recommend collecting around 10 oocytes, though the process can be repeated if needed.Gynecologist Rebeca Beguería said elite athletes do not return to peak physical condition immediately after treatment."The medical protocol states that normal life can be resumed, but for a high-performance athlete these are days when you do not perform at the same level: you will not run as fast or at the same intensity," she told EL Pais.She added that players face a greater risk of injury and abdominal damage during recovery."Your body's blood is redistributed; it is concentrated there; the abdomen and chest are more swollen, there is a tendency to migraines and fluid retention."Beguería also pointed out that while egg freezing helps players delay pregnancy, it does not remove the medical risks associated with becoming pregnant at an older age."Medically, the recommendation is that women get pregnant as early as possible, because biologically we are designed to be mothers by, at most, age 35 and we have extended that."The proposal has also highlighted the lack of regulations around fertility treatment in professional women's football.Lawyer Tania Tejeira wrote in an opinion piece in Palco23 that neither FIFA nor UEFA currently has a specific protocol covering treatments such as egg freezing or other assisted reproductive technologies, despite more players choosing these options.At present, the main international guidance comes from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), which requires medications used during fertility treatment to be reviewed and, where necessary, approved through a Therapeutic Use Exemption.
Article Summary: Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers. The move is aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level. The agreement is expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

That is what stayed with people.

Article Title: True Samaritans: Indian volunteers take up grim task of cleaning decomposed bodies in Kathmandu
Article Text:
Volunteers of Hemkunt Foundation cleaning floors of a morgue in Kathmandu. (PC: Hemkunt Foundation)

DEHRADUN:

As rescue agencies continue recovering bodies from flash flood-hit areas in Nepal and bringing them to Kathmandu mortuaries, a group of young Indian volunteers has taken up a task few are willing to do — cleaning decomposed bodies before they are handed over to families and authorities for the last rites. The group has helped clean more than 30 bodies till now.At least seven volunteers -- Harteerath Singh, Sonia Singh, Jag Singh, Jaskaran Singh, Ravi Singh, Amitose Singh and Harry Singh -- of Hemkunt Foundation, a Gurgaon-based non-profit organisation, are carrying out the work at the morgue of Maharajgunj Medical Campus, Kathmandu.One of the volunteers, Sonia Singh, told TOI Friday that she travelled from Mumbai to Kathmandu for the voluntary service after coming across a social media post by the foundation, requesting volunteers to join them in Nepal. “The next thing I did was to fly down to Kathmandu without expecting anything,” she said, adding that volunteers were not known to each other before reaching there; and were now working as a family in this ‘sewa’ (selfless service).They say that they are totally focused on the task, and even the terrible stench of bodies has failed to deter them. Sonia said, “We are here for the respect of the departed souls and the bereaved families.We don’t seek any publicity in that.”Another member of the group, Harteerath Singh, elaborated on some of the challenges being faced by them. “Due to the acute stench, sometimes, it becomes unbearable for us to stand inside the morgue even for a minute,” he pointed out.“But this is the ultimate ‘sewa’. At times, we don’t even bother to wear masks or gloves. We cover our faces with one corner of the turban cloth and just go inside to clean the bodies and floors of the morgue -- something which even the local authorities may not be willing to do,” Singh said.“We also see the positive side of it. It is the biggest opportunity for us to serve humanity.”
Article Summary: At least seven volunteers of hemkunt foundation, a gurgaon-based non-profit organisation, are carrying out the work at the morgue of maharajgunj medical campus, kathmandu. They say that they are totally focused on the task, and even the terrible stench of bodies has failed to deter them.
